## Structures of the Middle Ear

The **middle ear** (also called the tympanic cavity) is an air-filled space located within the petrous portion of the temporal bone, extending from the **tympanic membrane** (eardrum) to the lateral wall of the inner ear. It is structurally divided into two main parts:

### 1. **Tympanic Cavity**
The main chamber located directly medial to the tympanic membrane.

### 2. **Epitympanic Recess**
A space superior to the tympanic cavity where parts of the malleus and incus extend.

---

### Key Structures Within the Middle Ear:

| Structure | Description |
|-----------|-------------|
| **Auditory Ossicles** (3 bones) | The smallest bones in the human body that transmit sound vibrations |
| • **Malleus** (hammer) | Largest ossicle; attaches to the tympanic membrane |
| • **Incus** (anvil) | Middle ossicle; bridges the malleus and stapes |
| • **Stapes** (stirrup) | Smallest bone in the body; footplate fits into the oval window of the inner ear |
| **Tympanic Membrane** (Eardrum) | Separates the external ear from the middle ear; vibrates in response to sound waves |
| **Eustachian Tube** (Auditory/Pharyngotympanic Tube) | Connects the middle ear to the nasopharynx; equalizes air pressure |
| **Tensor Tympani Muscle** | Attaches to the malleus; tenses the eardrum to dampen loud sounds |
| **Stapedius Muscle** | Smallest skeletal muscle in the body; attaches to the stapes; stabilizes it in the oval window |
| **Mastoid Air Cells** | Air-filled spaces in the mastoid process that communicate with the middle ear |
| **Chorda Tympani Nerve** | Branch of the facial nerve (CN VII) that passes through the middle ear |
| **Tympanic Plexus** | Nerve network on the promontory from the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) |

---

### Function

The primary function of the middle ear is to **transmit and amplify sound vibrations** from the air-filled external environment to the fluid-filled inner ear. The ossicular chain (malleus → incus → stapes) acts as a lever system and impedance-matching device, amplifying sound pressure approximately **10 times** to prevent energy loss during this transfer.
